paragraphs: This paper studies changing patterns of brain activity using local field potentials recorded from several regions at once. These signals contain frequency patterns that can be correlated across regions. The authors model a brain state as something that influences the frequency content in each region, providing a way to describe coordinated activity over time.

The approach combines an infinite hidden Markov model for state transitions with Gaussian processes for the recorded signals. A state-dependent tensor factorization connects information across brain regions. Each region's signal is represented through a mixture of Gaussian processes, with mixture weights depending on both the region and the current state. The model estimates how many states and mixture components are needed.

The authors develop a variational Bayesian split-merge procedure to fit this model. On two datasets recorded simultaneously from multiple brain regions in mice, it infers state changes in relation to external covariates. Subject-matter experts validate and interpret the results, supporting the method's use for identifying meaningful patterns in these recordings.
neurips-2014-analysis-of-brain-states-fr.tldr: A probabilistic model identifies changing brain states from coordinated frequency patterns in recordings across multiple brain regions.

paragraphs: Recognizing an object's category does not by itself establish which parts correspond across different images. This paper asks whether convolutional networks trained with whole-image labels also learn features useful for such finer spatial matching. The question matters because large pooling regions could make features effective for recognition while leaving their ability to locate precise details uncertain.

The authors examine network activation features on tasks that require correspondence. Their evidence indicates that these features can localize image content at a scale much finer than the regions of the input that influence them. Thus, a large receptive field does not, in the tested setting, prevent a feature from carrying more precise spatial information.

The study also finds that these features support alignment between objects of the same category as well as conventional hand-engineered features. For predicting object keypoints on PASCAL VOC 2011, they outperform conventional features. Together, these findings show that representations learned for broad recognition can also be useful for matching and locating object details.
neurips-2014-do-convnets-learn-correspon.tldr: Convolutional network features show precise localization and useful correspondence despite training with whole-image labels.

paragraphs: Partial monitoring describes sequential decisions in which the learner receives only limited feedback about outcomes. Each chosen action incurs a loss and produces feedback determined jointly by that action and the opponent's outcome. The paper studies how prior information about the opponent's outcome distribution can help the learner keep cumulative loss low.

The proposed BPM family of algorithms tracks the outcome distribution using an ellipsoid centered on its current estimate. This representation allows the algorithms to organize uncertainty around what they have learned while incorporating prior information. The central computational task is therefore to maintain and use an evolving description of the distribution behind the observed feedback.

For locally observable partial-monitoring problems with stochastic opponents, the authors prove near-optimal regret rates. This guarantee applies to that specified class of problems and opponents. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data report lower running time and regret an order of magnitude smaller than previous approaches, even with very uninformed priors. The findings suggest that the framework can remain useful when prior knowledge is weak.
neurips-2014-efficient-partial-monitorin.tldr: BPM uses prior information and ellipsoidal uncertainty estimates to learn efficiently from limited feedback, with near-optimal guarantees in a specified stochastic setting.

paragraphs: Feature selection can use known relationships among features by organizing them into groups. Standard group lasso encourages sparsity between groups, allowing some groups to be excluded together. This paper introduces exclusive group lasso to encourage sparsity within groups instead, changing which level of the feature structure the selection process targets.

The formulation accommodates both overlapping and non-overlapping feature groups. This matters when a feature belongs to several meaningful collections, because the method does not require those collections to form a disjoint partition. The authors analyze properties of the formulation and develop an iteratively reweighted algorithm for solving its optimization problem, together with a rigorous convergence analysis.

The paper applies the approach to selecting uncorrelated features, connecting within-group sparsity to the goal of choosing less redundant information. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets indicate good performance. The contribution combines a different structural preference for feature selection with an optimization method whose convergence is analyzed, making the grouping information useful in a more flexible way.
neurips-2014-exclusive-feature-learning-.tldr: Exclusive group lasso encourages sparse selection within potentially overlapping feature groups and comes with a convergence-analyzed optimization algorithm.

paragraphs: When several agents have their own interests, a policy that achieves strong total performance can still leave some agents doing poorly. This paper defines a fairness criterion for sequential decision-making that aims to improve the worst agent performance while also considering overall performance. It makes the distribution of outcomes among agents part of the optimization objective.

The authors give two methods for computing an optimal fairness policy. One uses linear programming. The other recasts the optimization as a two-player zero-sum game and iteratively searches for a Nash equilibrium corresponding to an optimal fairness policy. Exploiting problem structure and approximating value functions makes the game-based approach more scalable.

Experiments on resource allocation problems find that the proposed criterion produces a more favorable solution than the utilitarian criterion under the study's evaluation. They also show that the game-theoretic method is significantly faster than linear programming. The results connect a specific notion of fairness to a practical computational approach, rather than treating fairness solely as a property assessed after choosing a policy.
neurips-2014-fairness-in-multi-agent-seq.tldr: A fairness objective considers worst-agent and overall performance, with a game-theoretic solver that is faster than linear programming in resource allocation experiments.

paragraphs: Data measured across locations and times can contain several variables whose patterns are related. This paper addresses the challenge of modeling these dependencies accurately without making computation prohibitively expensive. It proposes a unified low-rank tensor learning framework, using a multidimensional representation to connect the variable, spatial, and temporal aspects of the data.

The framework can incorporate properties such as spatial clustering and structure shared among variables. These capabilities matter because relationships in the data need not be captured adequately by simple assumptions about how space, time, and variables interact. The authors show how the framework supports both cokriging, which concerns spatial estimation using related variables, and forecasting.

To fit the resulting models, the paper develops an efficient greedy algorithm with a convergence guarantee. Experiments on synthetic and real application datasets show significantly faster computation and lower estimation error than existing methods in the comparisons reported. The findings support the combination of a flexible shared representation and an efficient optimization procedure for the examined spatiotemporal analysis tasks.
neurips-2014-fast-multivariate-spatio-te.tldr: A low-rank tensor framework captures shared spatiotemporal structure and achieves faster computation with lower estimation error in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Recovering the three-dimensional shape of a deforming object from a single-camera video becomes difficult when tracking is incomplete or the object is mixed with its surroundings. This paper brings non-rigid structure-from-motion toward these more realistic conditions by combining dense optical-flow tracking, clustering of motion trajectories, and three-dimensional reconstruction.

For each trajectory cluster, the method computes multiple reconstructions under different bounds on the trajectory matrix's rank. It minimizes both reprojection error, which measures consistency with the observed images, and the rank of the reconstructed shape. Grouping and reconstruction therefore work with the incomplete motion evidence available in the video.

The authors show dense shape recovery and completion of trajectories through occlusions and regions with little texture, including cases with mild relative motion between object and camera. They report competitive performance on a public benchmark using fixed parameters across sequences and incomplete trajectories, and further tests on video segmentation datasets. The method also extracts dense object models from realistic videos without object-specific priors, which the authors describe as a first to their knowledge.
neurips-2014-grouping-based-low-rank-tra.tldr: Combining motion grouping with low-rank reconstruction enables dense three-dimensional object recovery from realistic videos with incomplete trajectories.

paragraphs: This paper experimentally examines how reusable a deep convolutional network's features are at different layers. Early features often resemble broadly useful visual patterns, whereas later features must serve the original task more specifically. The study measures this transition and investigates what makes transferring parts of a trained network difficult.

It identifies two distinct obstacles: specialization to the source task and optimization difficulties caused by separating neurons that have adapted to work together. In an example network trained on ImageNet, either obstacle can dominate depending on where features are transferred from. Thus, reduced transfer performance need not be explained solely by features becoming too specific.

The experiments also find that transferability decreases as source and target tasks become more distant, although even distant-task features can outperform random features. Initializing with transferred features from almost any number of layers can improve generalization, with benefits persisting after fine-tuning on the target dataset. These results show that both task similarity and interactions among learned layers influence the value of reuse.
neurips-2014-how-transferable-are-featur.tldr: Feature transfer depends on task specialization and interactions among neurons, while transferred initialization can retain benefits after fine-tuning.

paragraphs: The paper explores whether learning can help discover mathematical expressions that compute the same quantity more efficiently. Its objective is analytical equivalence to a target expression together with lower computational complexity. This makes the search about finding useful mathematical identities, rather than merely producing expressions that resemble the target on selected inputs.

An attribute grammar represents expressions as trees assembled from mathematical operators. Searching these trees directly becomes impractical because the number of possible combinations grows exponentially with expression complexity. The authors therefore introduce two ways to learn from simpler expressions and use that knowledge to guide searches for more complex ones.

One approach uses an n-gram model, while the other uses a recursive neural network. Both supply learned guidance to the symbolic tree search. The authors report that these approaches derive complex identities they describe as beyond the reach of brute-force search or human derivation. The contribution is a combination of structured symbolic representation and learned search guidance for finding computationally cheaper equivalent expressions.
neurips-2014-learning-to-discover-effici.tldr: Learned models guide symbolic tree search toward analytically equivalent mathematical expressions with lower computational complexity.

paragraphs: Branch-and-bound solves combinatorial optimization problems by exploring a tree of candidate subproblems. The order in which it visits nodes is an important part of that search. This paper addresses how to learn an adaptive node-searching strategy systematically, a question the authors distinguish from developing specialized techniques for individual optimization problems.

The proposed strategies are trained through imitation learning. The intended framework applies to problem classes solvable by branch-and-bound, while the concrete application uses branch-and-bound based on linear programming to solve mixed integer programs. Learning focuses on the order of exploration within the optimization procedure.

The authors compare their approach with SCIP, an open-source solver, and Gurobi, a commercial solver. Across four mixed integer programming libraries, they report obtaining better solutions faster. This is evidence for the value of learned search order in the tested settings. The broader contribution is to make a search strategy something that can be learned for a problem class, rather than relying entirely on manually designed choices.
neurips-2014-learning-to-search-in-branc.tldr: Imitation learning produces adaptive branch-and-bound search orders that find better solutions faster in tests on four mixed integer programming libraries.

paragraphs: A sample can have several feature representations because it is measured through different data sources. Multiview learning aims to combine these representations into a useful analysis. This paper focuses on clustering and asks how the contribution of different sources can reflect characteristics of individual samples.

The authors extend kernel k-means with a multiple-kernel learning algorithm. Each view supplies a kernel describing relationships among samples, and the method combines these kernels locally. This gives the data fusion process a way to account for sample-specific characteristics, rather than requiring the same global combination to describe the entire dataset.

The approach is evaluated by clustering patients in a human colon and rectal cancer dataset. Relative to global data fusion methods, it finds patient groups with greater prognostic relevance when assessed against three commonly used clinical biomarkers. The reported result supports localized fusion for this clustering application: allowing the integration of data sources to vary across samples can reveal clinically relevant groupings that a global combination captures less effectively.
neurips-2014-localized-data-fusion-for-k.tldr: Locally combining kernels from multiple data sources yields more prognostically relevant patient clusters than global fusion in the reported cancer dataset.

paragraphs: Visual cortical responses reflect both incoming stimuli and ongoing activity within neural circuits. This paper introduces a statistical population model that combines a nonlinear receptive-field model with a latent dynamical model. The aim is to explain how stimulus responses interact with shared internal dynamics across many recorded neurons.

The model captures temporal patterns, effective network connectivity, and correlations arising from shared stimulus input and common noise. Its key representational idea is that ongoing dynamics mix nonlinear stimulus inputs. A relatively small set of inputs can therefore account for many distinct receptive-field shapes through a low-dimensional dynamical system.

The authors develop a fast fitting procedure using online expectation maximization with Laplace approximations. Inference scales linearly with both the number of neurons and recording duration, making the computational claim directly relevant to large recordings. Applied to multichannel primary visual cortex data, the model accounts for many individual receptive fields with few nonlinear inputs and low-dimensional dynamics. This supports a compact joint description of stimulus sensitivity and ongoing population activity.
neurips-2014-low-dimensional-models-of-n.tldr: A compact dynamical model combines visual inputs and ongoing cortical activity to explain many neurons' receptive fields with scalable inference.

paragraphs: The paper studies related prediction tasks indexed by pairs such as consumer and time. Each task has a weight vector, and these vectors form a tensor. The tensor's multilinear rank controls how much information tasks share, connecting multitask learning with the problem of finding low-rank multidimensional structure.

The authors argue that two existing convex relaxations of multilinear rank are not optimal for multitask settings with unequal dimensions or differing ranks across tensor directions. They introduce the scaled latent trace norm to address this heterogeneity. They then analyze excess risk for the new norm and the two existing alternatives.

The analysis covers settings including matrix completion, tensor completion, multitask learning, and multilinear multitask learning. Both theoretical results and experiments support the new norm's advantage when tensor dimensions are unequal and the low-rank direction is not known beforehand. This qualification is central to the contribution: the proposed regularizer is motivated by uncertainty about where useful shared structure lies in an unevenly shaped collection of tasks.
neurips-2014-multitask-learning-meets-te.tldr: The scaled latent trace norm improves supported multitask and completion settings with unequal tensor dimensions and an unknown low-rank direction.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a two-layer spiking neural network that approximately infers and learns a hidden Markov model. Sensory neurons receive noisy measurements of an unobserved world state. A recurrent upper layer uses their spike trains to infer a probability distribution over possible states, allowing the model to represent uncertainty.

Each spike in the inference population acts as a sample of a particular hidden state. Activity across the population approximates the posterior distribution through a process similar to Monte Carlo methods such as particle filtering. Variability in spike timing supplies the randomness needed for sampling, offering a functional explanation for Poisson-like variability in cortical responses.

The network does not require sensory neurons to observe the hidden state directly, and the state's temporal dynamics are initially unknown. The authors demonstrate sequential learning of the hidden Markov model through a spike-timing-dependent Hebbian rule, with power-law convergence rates. The result links approximate probabilistic inference and learning to a common mechanism built from spikes, recurrent connections, and synaptic plasticity.
neurips-2014-neurons-as-monte-carlo-samp.tldr: A two-layer spiking network uses spikes as samples to approximately infer hidden states and learn their unknown dynamics.

paragraphs: People's category decisions can depend on a small, randomly retrieved set of remembered examples. This limited retrieval helps explain why training examples that reduce the prominence of ambiguous cases can improve later judgments. The paper seeks a principled way to construct these idealized training sets, replacing the heuristic choices used in previous work.

The authors apply machine teaching to cognitive models with either limited or unlimited capacity. The teacher selects training recommendations according to the assumed learner. It recommends idealized training sets, connecting the structure of the examples to the learner's capacity constraints rather than treating idealization as an arbitrary adjustment.

Human learners perform best when the teacher's recommendations come from a limited-capacity model. The findings support the prediction that teaching becomes effective to the extent that its learner model matches human learning. They provide a normative justification for idealization under capacity constraints and suggest a way to assess models of human learning through the effectiveness of the teaching recommendations those models generate.
neurips-2014-optimal-teaching-for-limite.tldr: Machine teaching produces more effective human training examples when its learner model accounts for limited memory retrieval.

paragraphs: F-measures are nonlinear classification objectives, so improving them is not simply the same problem as reducing an ordinary error count. This paper analyzes F-measures in binary, multiclass, and multilabel settings. Its central observation is that, in many scenarios, these measures have a pseudo-linear structure in the rates of false positives and false negatives.

Using that structure, the authors reduce F-measure maximization to cost-sensitive classification with initially unknown costs. They propose an algorithm that solves a sequence of classification problems assigning different costs to errors. The algorithm has provable guarantees for obtaining a classifier that is approximately optimal for the F-measure.

The analysis applies to any dataset and any classifier class within the scope of the reduction, extending prior results described as asymptotic. Numerical experiments with linear classifiers examine the relative importance of asymmetric error costs and thresholding across F-measure tasks. The contribution explains how an objective with nonlinear error tradeoffs can be approached through a series of cost-sensitive learning problems.
neurips-2014-optimizing-f-measures-by-co.tldr: A structural analysis reduces supported F-measure optimization problems to sequences of cost-sensitive classification tasks with approximation guarantees.

paragraphs: Statistical estimation usually asks how accurately a signal can be recovered from noisy observations. This paper adds a resource constraint: the estimator must be encoded using a limited number of bits. The question becomes how estimation accuracy changes when the result must fit within a storage or communication budget.

The authors extend Pinsker's theorem, a minimax result for the normal means model, to this constrained setting. They analyze excess risk as a function of the bit budget, signal size, and noise level. These quantities jointly describe the statistical problem and the resources available to represent its answer.

For signals in a Euclidean ball, the paper establishes sharp upper and lower bounds. The upper bounds describe attainable performance, while the lower bounds establish limits that estimators cannot surpass in the minimax sense. Together, they characterize the Pareto-optimal tradeoff between storage and risk for this setting. The contribution makes the cost of representing an estimate part of the theoretical account of estimation accuracy.
neurips-2014-quantized-estimation-of-gau.tldr: Sharp bounds characterize the optimal minimax tradeoff between encoding bits and estimation risk for Gaussian sequence models in Euclidean balls.

paragraphs: This paper studies logistic regression when the covariate matrix, which contains the input features, includes arbitrary outliers. The corruption is allowed to be adversarial, so robustness must address more than ordinary random variation in the measurements. The central problem is estimating the model's parameter despite these damaged inputs.

The authors introduce RoLR, a robust logistic regression algorithm that estimates the parameter through a simple linear programming procedure. They prove robustness to a constant fraction of adversarial outliers. This gives the method a performance guarantee in a setting where some of the feature information may have been corrupted deliberately.

The authors describe this as, to their knowledge, the first guaranteed result for logistic regression parameter estimation with a corrupted covariate matrix. They also apply RoLR to binary classification when a fraction of training samples are corrupted. The contribution therefore links a computationally specified estimation procedure and a robustness proof to the practical task of learning a two-category decision rule from contaminated training data.
neurips-2014-robust-logistic-regression-.tldr: RoLR uses linear programming to estimate logistic regression parameters with proven robustness to a constant fraction of adversarial outliers.

paragraphs: This paper presents an end-to-end method for mapping an input sequence to an output sequence with minimal assumptions about sequence structure. A multilayer LSTM encodes the input into a fixed-dimensional vector, and a second deep LSTM decodes the target sequence. The vector connects the two learned stages.

On WMT-14 English-to-French translation, the model achieves 34.8 BLEU on the full test set, including penalties for out-of-vocabulary words, compared with 33.3 for a phrase-based statistical translation system. Using the LSTM to rerank that system's 1,000 candidate translations raises the score to 36.5, close to the previous state of the art. The authors also report no difficulty with long sentences.

The learned representations are sensitive to word order while being relatively insensitive to active versus passive voice. Reversing source sentences, while leaving target sentences unchanged, markedly improves performance. The authors attribute this improvement to shorter dependencies between source and target, which make optimization easier. The findings show how both the encoder-decoder design and input ordering affect the reported translation results.
neurips-2014-sequence-to-sequence-learni.tldr: An LSTM encoder-decoder learns sequence mappings and achieves strong translation results, with substantial improvement from reversing source-word order.

paragraphs: Social network activity can arise from users responding to their neighbors or from influences outside the network. This paper asks how much external drive to direct toward each user to move overall activity toward a desired level. Answering that question requires accounting for the activity that external influences can trigger through social responses.

The authors model events with multivariate Hawkes processes, which represent both external activity and activity generated through interactions within the network. They derive a time-dependent linear relationship between external event intensity and total network activity. This relationship connects an adjustable input to its modeled effects across the network over time.

Using that connection, the paper develops a convex optimization framework for selecting the external drive needed to reach an activity target. Experiments using event data from Twitter show more accurate steering than the alternatives tested. The contribution turns a model of interacting social events into a planning method, using the relationship between direct stimulation and induced responses to choose how external influence is allocated.
neurips-2014-shaping-social-activity-by-.tldr: A Hawkes-process model and convex optimization allocate external drive to steer social network activity toward a target.

paragraphs: Neural transmission and processing introduce delays, creating a challenge for tracking moving stimuli in time. This paper proposes that spike-frequency adaptation, a widely observed property of neuronal responses, can support anticipatory tracking. The authors study the mechanism in continuous attractor neural networks used to model tracking behavior.

Adding adaptation gives the network intrinsic mobility: it can sustain traveling waves of activity without their movement being entirely imposed by the stimulus. When a moving stimulus drives the network, tracking depends on the interaction between that external drive and the network's own motion. The anticipation regime effectively coincides with conditions where the intrinsic wave speed exceeds the stimulus drive's speed.

Depending on adaptation amplitude, the model can track with zero lag or maintain a constant lead over the input. It also reproduces experimentally observed anticipatory tracking behaviors. These findings support adaptation as a possible mechanism for timely motion processing, with the particular tracking behavior depending on the balance between intrinsic network dynamics and the moving external signal.
neurips-2014-spike-frequency-adaptation-.tldr: Spike-frequency adaptation gives a neural tracking model intrinsic motion that can produce zero-lag or anticipatory tracking under suitable conditions.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential learning when changing actions temporarily removes feedback. Such a setting can arise when the environment needs time to settle after a change. The authors formalize it as a blinded multi-armed bandit problem, where switching arms means the learner receives no feedback at the switch.

They develop efficient algorithms and prove that these attain the same asymptotic regret as optimal algorithms for the standard multi-armed bandit problem. Regret expresses the performance shortfall associated with learning which actions to take. The result shows that the specified feedback loss can be handled without worsening its optimal asymptotic rate.

The paper contrasts this finding with a result in which charging a switching cost makes the standard bandit problem substantially harder. Losing information when switching and directly increasing loss when switching can therefore affect learning difficulty differently. The authors also extend their approach to bandit linear optimization, obtaining near-optimal regret bounds there. This broadens the analysis beyond choosing among individual arms to a more general prediction framework.
neurips-2014-the-blinded-bandit-learning.tldr: Efficient bandit algorithms tolerate feedback loss when switching actions while retaining the standard problem's optimal asymptotic regret rate.

paragraphs: A cluster can have a skewed shape or several peaks, making a single Gaussian an inadequate description. The paper explains that a Dirichlet process mixture of Gaussians can then split a relatively well-defined cluster into several extra clusters. It proposes a model that separates the flexibility needed within a cluster from the identification of clusters themselves.

The infinite mixture of infinite Gaussian mixtures assigns a whole Dirichlet process Gaussian mixture to each cluster. These individual mixtures are linked through a higher-level Dirichlet process prior that determines the centers of their base distributions. This hierarchy allows a cluster's distribution to be represented by multiple Gaussian components.

Inference uses a collapsed Gibbs sampler that permits partial parallelization. Experiments on artificial and real-world datasets suggest more accurate cluster prediction than the tested variational Bayes and Gibbs-sampling versions of the standard model. The findings support the proposed distinction between a meaningful cluster and the Gaussian components needed to describe its internal shape, particularly for skewed and multimodal cluster distributions.
neurips-2014-the-infinite-mixture-of-inf.tldr: A hierarchical mixture model lets each cluster contain multiple Gaussian components, improving flexibility for skewed and multimodal cluster shapes.

paragraphs: This paper examines a tradeoff between the amount of data available and the computation needed for statistical estimation. It focuses on estimators defined through convex optimization. The central proposal is that a larger dataset can make it possible to change the optimization problem more aggressively while still obtaining an accurate estimate.

The mechanism is smoothing: as data increases, the optimization problem can be smoothed more strongly so that accurate estimates can be reached more quickly. The relevant goal is statistical accuracy, linking how the optimization is carried out to the information available in the observations. This connects sample requirements and computational effort within the same estimation problem.

The authors provide both theoretical and experimental evidence for this tradeoff in a class of regularized linear inverse problems. The stated scope matters: the evidence concerns that class, while the broader proposal addresses convex-optimization-based estimation. Its significance is that additional data can support a computational advantage through a different optimization strategy, making the amount of data relevant to how aggressively an estimator's objective is smoothed.
neurips-2014-time-data-tradeoffs-by-aggr.tldr: More data can permit stronger smoothing of convex estimation problems, yielding accurate estimates with less computation in the studied setting.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether EEG recorded during rhythm perception contains enough information to identify the rhythm being heard. The study uses recordings from 13 participants in Kigali, Rwanda, exposed to 12 East African and 12 Western rhythms. Each stimulus was repeated in a loop for 32 seconds.

The authors apply convolutional neural networks to classify the EEG and examine how data representation, preprocessing, and network structure affect the task. The reported single-channel result uses less than three seconds of signal. Across subjects, mean accuracy for recognizing individual rhythms reaches 24.4%, compared with a chance level of 4.17%.

Combining predictions from multiple channels can raise mean accuracy to as much as 50% for individual subjects. That result concerns individual subjects and is distinct from the average across all subjects for the single-channel setting. Together, the findings show that the recorded EEG carries information useful for distinguishing the presented rhythms and that aggregating channels can improve recognition in the reported cases.
neurips-2014-using-convolutional-neural-.tldr: CNNs identify presented rhythms from short EEG segments above chance, with further gains from combining channels for individual subjects.
